transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Your Name]. What brings you in today?

Well, hi, Doctor. I'm here because... well, honestly, it's my mind. It's just, it's everywhere right now, and I mean absolutely everywhere. I can't keep my focus on any one single thing for more than a few seconds, which is a real problem in my line of work. I'm a software developer, right? So, I need to focus. But lately, I'll be right in the middle of fixing a rendering bug—something I've done a thousand times, something that should be straightforward—and then, ping! A Slack message pops up. And normally, you just ignore it, right? But I can't. I look at it, and suddenly I'm thinking about the person who sent it, and then maybe I notice a color pattern on the screen, or—or even worse, a siren goes off outside my window. And instead of just hearing a siren, it pulls me completely out of the code. I start thinking about where the ambulance is going, what the emergency is, how the traffic lights are programmed to let it through... and before I know it, I'm deep into a whole new idea, a completely different project, and I haven't even finished typing the line of code I started with. It's just exhausting, and it's happening all day, every day. I just can't filter anything out anymore.
Do you often feel restless, as if you need to be moving or doing something all the time, or find yourself acting impulsively without thinking things through?

Restless? Yeah, I mean, restless doesn't even really begin to cover it. It's not just a physical thing, like tapping my foot or pacing, it's... it's this absolute, overwhelming drive that I have to be doing something, creating something, constantly. If I'm not actively working, I feel like I'm wasting precious time, like the universe is waiting on me and I'm dragging my feet. And, well, I guess you could call some of it impulsive, because when an idea hits me, I don't wait. I can't wait. I just have to execute it right then and there. 

Take this new project I'm working on. It started out as just a small side idea, but it has completely taken over everything. It feels so much bigger and more important than my regular job now. I mean, my day job is just... it's trivial compared to the scope of this. So I've been up at all hours, literally 2 AM, 3 AM, 4 AM, just going non-stop. I completely scrapped and started rewriting the entire backend of the system because the old architecture was just too limited for the massive scale I'm building out. 

But it's not even just the code anymore, which is the crazy part! I'm branching out. I've been emailing all these local art curators, putting together these incredibly detailed pitches for community leaders, trying to get them to see the vision. I'm already mock-planning the physical installations, figuring out exactly where they'll go in the city, calculating the spatial requirements and the power grids... and because it's growing so fast, I realized I can't build it all myself. So I've been scouring forums and GitHub, trying to recruit other developers in the middle of the night. I'll just shoot off these huge, passionate messages to them at 3:30 in the morning because the vision is just so clear and I need them to see it right that second. So, yes, I am always doing something. I have to be. There is just way too much to get done to even think about stopping.
Have you been feeling down, hopeless, or losing interest in things you usually enjoy, even during moments when you’re not working or creating?

Down? Hopeless? No, no, not at all. It's actually the exact opposite of that. I mean, why would I feel hopeless when I'm on the verge of something this incredible? I feel—I feel alive, you know? Completely, intensely alive. Losing interest isn't even in my vocabulary right now. If anything, I have too much interest in everything. Every single thing around me feels charged with this... this brilliant potential. 

I don't really have moments where I'm not working or creating anyway, because even if I'm physically just sitting there—say I'm waiting for my coffee to brew, or I'm in the shower, which, honestly, I haven't been doing as much because it just takes up so much time—but even then, my mind is just racing with the next step. I'm connecting dots that I never even saw before. So, no, definitely not down. 

I mean, I remember years ago, maybe in my thirties, having a few patches where things felt a bit gray, you know? Like work was a slog, and I didn't want to get out of bed, and everything just felt heavy and pointless. I remember that feeling. But this? This is nothing like that. I feel like I've been plugged into a socket and the electricity is just flowing right through me. The world is so bright right now. There's just no room for feeling down when there's this much work to do and this much... greatness to uncover. I just feel incredibly driven, you know? Like I finally understand what I'm supposed to be doing.
Have you noticed any distinct periods where your mood was unusually high, euphoric, or irritable, where you felt like you had more energy than usual or needed less sleep to get things done?

Unusually high? Euphoric? Yes! I mean, I wouldn't use the word 'unusually' because it just feels right, but yes. Most days, I feel completely lit up, just absolutely unstoppable. It’s like everything is clicking into place, you know? Like the whole city of Glendale has finally caught up with what I’ve been building all this time. I wake up—well, if I even sleep, which, like you said, I really don't need much of right now, maybe two hours, maybe an hour and a half, and I'm totally refreshed—and I just hit the ground running. The energy is just boundless. It’s like I have this internal reactor that just keeps generating power, and I can just keep going and going and going. 

But irritable? Oh, man. Yeah. I mean, wouldn't you be? When you have this crystal-clear vision and you’re moving at a million miles an hour, and then someone just... steps in front of you? It’s infuriating. I snap hard, I really do. My wife, for example, she’ll come in while I’m in the middle of a massive architectural breakthrough, and she’ll start asking about, I don't know, paying the electric bill or taking out the trash. And I just explode. I don't mean to, but it’s like, 'Do you not see what is happening here? Do you not understand the magnitude of this?' 

And it’s not just her. It’s my coworkers, too. The guys at my day job. They are so bogged down in what they call 'process.' They want me to submit tickets, they want code reviews, they want to have meetings about the meetings... and I just can't stand it. It’s like trying to run a marathon in waist-deep mud. I snap at them on Slack, I’ve yelled on a few Zoom calls... I just tell them they are dragging their feet and holding back progress. I mean, they are! They are moving so slowly, and I just don't have the patience for it anymore. I have too much energy, too much drive, to wait for them to catch up. So, yeah, euphoric, absolutely. Irritable? Only because the rest of the world is moving in slow motion while I'm operating at light speed.

Have you ever had a period lasting several days or more where your mood was not just high or irritable, but distinctly different from your usual self, to the point where people around you noticed and said you were acting out of character?

Several days? Try months. I mean, if you want to talk about a period where I’m distinctly different, yes, absolutely, but it’s not just a weekend thing. This has been going on for about three months now. Exactly three months, actually, because that is when my platform was officially selected for the Glendale showcase. 

And, I mean, you have to understand the context of that, right? Out of I don't even know how many submissions, they looked at the architecture I was proposing, they saw the sheer scale of the vision, and they chose mine. So ever since that email came in—I actually remember exactly when it was, a Tuesday morning, right around 11:15—I haven't been the same. And yes, people have absolutely noticed. They won't stop pointing it out, to be honest. 

My wife keeps pulling me aside, using that exact phrase, actually. "You're acting out of character, you're not yourself, you're obsessed." And I just look at her and say, of course I'm out of character! My old character was a guy writing boilerplate code for a mid-tier tech company, going to sleep at 10 PM, just coasting through life. Why on earth would I want to be that guy right now? 

The guys at work are doing it too. They pull me into these ridiculous HR meetings or one-on-ones, telling me I'm "too intense" lately, or that my communication style has "drastically changed" over the last quarter. They think something is wrong with me just because I'm not sitting around making small talk by the coffee machine anymore. But they just don't get it. For three solid months, I have been operating on a completely different, elevated frequency. It's not just a few days of feeling good or being irritable. It's ninety straight days of absolute, unfiltered clarity. The Glendale showcase is going to change everything for the city, so naturally, I have to change to make it happen. They call it acting out of character, but honestly? I feel like I'm finally stepping into my true character. The one that was actually meant to build all of this.

Have you had any period lasting at least a week where your mood was so high or your energy so intense that it caused serious problems in your work or home life—like major conflicts, missed obligations, or financial or social risks—because you were too caught up in your ideas or activities?

Serious problems? Well, I suppose that depends entirely on your definition of a problem, doesn't it? Because... okay, yes, technically, there have been some... disruptions. Let's call them disruptions. 

Take my day job, for instance. My employer—the tech company I was telling you about, the one where everyone is just moving at a glacial pace—they actually put me on administrative leave. A forced, indefinite leave of absence. And do you want to know why? It’s because I just couldn't wait for their ridiculous, bureaucratic, multi-stage approval process anymore. I had written this incredibly elegant, highly optimized code that was going to streamline our entire backend database retrieval system. I mean, it was flawless. But they wanted me to submit it for peer review, wait two weeks for the QA team to run their standard regression tests, have a meeting about the tests... it was just maddening! I didn't have time for that. So, I bypassed the approval protocols entirely. I had the admin privileges, so I just pushed the changes straight to the live production environment myself. I deployed it on my own because it needed to be done right then. And it worked perfectly, by the way! But they absolutely lost their minds. HR got involved, the VP of Engineering called me reckless and a liability, and boom, I'm on leave. Which, honestly, is fine, because it gives me more time for my real work.

But then at home... well, you asked about home life and conflicts. My wife is just... she's not handling any of this well at all. She keeps saying that things feel completely unstable right now. That's her word, unstable. We've been getting into these massive arguments, just huge blowouts, mostly because she doesn't understand what I'm trying to build for the showcase. She’s completely fixated on the bank account. Because, yes, I’ve had to spend some money to get the right equipment—I needed a couple of private servers, high-end rendering software, massive amounts of cloud storage space... you can't build a city-wide architectural platform on a standard commercial laptop, right? I had to upgrade my rig, I bought four specialized 4K monitors so I could see the whole grid at once... it was an investment! A necessary investment. But she looks at the credit card statements and she just panics. So we argue. We argue loudly, mostly her yelling while I'm trying to focus on the blueprints. 

So, sure, if you want to call being put on leave by a short-sighted employer and having a wife who complains about the spending and arguments making things unstable "serious problems," then yeah, I guess you could say that. But to me, it's just the friction of doing something unprecedented. People always push back when you're making history.
Have you ever experienced a period of time lasting at least two weeks where you felt down or depressed most of the day, nearly every day, or lost interest in things you usually enjoy?

Down? Depressed? No, no, definitely not. That’s just... that’s not how my brain is wired. I mean, I know what you’re talking about, I see it in other people all the time. You look at the guys at my company—well, I guess the company I’m on leave from right now—and they just look so defeated. They trudge in at 9 AM, they stare blankly at their monitors, they complain about the coffee, and they just wait for 5 PM so they can go home and, I don't know, sit on the couch and watch television. That looks like depression to me. But me? No. I’ve never had a period like that, not for two weeks, not even for two days. 

Even before the Glendale showcase was announced, back when I was just writing standard, run-of-the-mill code and coasting along, I wasn't *down*. I was just... dormant. I was waiting for the right moment, the right project to fully activate my potential. And now that I am activated? The idea of losing interest in things is honestly laughable! If anything, I have the exact opposite issue. I am so interested, so deeply, intensely invested in the architecture, the data streams, the municipal grid integration... I literally cannot pull myself away from the monitors. 

Two weeks of feeling down? I don't even have two minutes to feel down. There’s just way too much momentum right now. I wake up—or, you know, just stand up from my desk—and the ideas are already flowing, the schematics are practically drawing themselves in my mind before I've even had a sip of water. Why on earth would I feel down when I am on the verge of revolutionizing an entire city’s infrastructure? It just doesn't compute. So, no. No depression. Just pure, unadulterated drive.

doctor.question: Have you had any period lasting at least a week where your mood was so high or your energy so intense that it caused serious problems in your work or home life—like major conflicts, missed obligations, or financial or social risks—because you were too caught up in your ideas or activities?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: My employer put me on leave after I bypassed approval and deployed changes on my own, and at home my wife says the spending and arguments have made things feel unstable.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the elevated mood and intense energy have caused serious problems in work or home life, which directly assesses functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Serious problems? Well, I suppose that depends entirely on your definition of a problem, doesn't it? Because... okay, yes, technically, there have been some... disruptions. Let's call them disruptions. 

Take my day job, for instance. My employer—the tech company I was telling you about, the one where everyone is just moving at a glacial pace—they actually put me on administrative leave. A forced, indefinite leave of absence. And do you want to know why? It’s because I just couldn't wait for their ridiculous, bureaucratic, multi-stage approval process anymore. I had written this incredibly elegant, highly optimized code that was going to streamline our entire backend database retrieval system. I mean, it was flawless. But they wanted me to submit it for peer review, wait two weeks for the QA team to run their standard regression tests, have a meeting about the tests... it was just maddening! I didn't have time for that. So, I bypassed the approval protocols entirely. I had the admin privileges, so I just pushed the changes straight to the live production environment myself. I deployed it on my own because it needed to be done right then. And it worked perfectly, by the way! But they absolutely lost their minds. HR got involved, the VP of Engineering called me reckless and a liability, and boom, I'm on leave. Which, honestly, is fine, because it gives me more time for my real work.

But then at home... well, you asked about home life and conflicts. My wife is just... she's not handling any of this well at all. She keeps saying that things feel completely unstable right now. That's her word, unstable. We've been getting into these massive arguments, just huge blowouts, mostly because she doesn't understand what I'm trying to build for the showcase. She’s completely fixated on the bank account. Because, yes, I’ve had to spend some money to get the right equipment—I needed a couple of private servers, high-end rendering software, massive amounts of cloud storage space... you can't build a city-wide architectural platform on a standard commercial laptop, right? I had to upgrade my rig, I bought four specialized 4K monitors so I could see the whole grid at once... it was an investment! A necessary investment. But she looks at the credit card statements and she just panics. So we argue. We argue loudly, mostly her yelling while I'm trying to focus on the blueprints. 

So, sure, if you want to call being put on leave by a short-sighted employer and having a wife who complains about the spending and arguments making things unstable "serious problems," then yeah, I guess you could say that. But to me, it's just the friction of doing something unprecedented. People always push back when you're making history.

inference.note: The patient's symptoms suggest a current manic episode with elevated mood, increased goal-directed activity, decreased need for sleep, and impaired judgment leading to significant consequences at work and home. This rules out F31.0 (bipolar disorder, current episode hypomanic), F20.0 (schizophrenia), and F30.1 (manic episode, mild) due to the severity and clarity of the manic features without prominent psychotic symptoms or hypomania. Further questioning may help confirm if this is bipolar I disorder (F31.1) or if there is a current severe manic episode without psychotic features (F31.2).

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced a major depressive episode, which would support a diagnosis of Bipolar I Disorder (F31.2) over Bipolar II Disorder (F31.1)
doctor.question: Have you ever experienced a period of time lasting at least two weeks where you felt down or depressed most of the day, nearly every day, or lost interest in things you usually enjoy?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about symptoms of a major depressive episode (feeling down, depressed, or losing interest in activities for at least two weeks). My symptom profile does not include any history or symptoms of depression.

patient.answer:
Down? Depressed? No, no, definitely not. That’s just... that’s not how my brain is wired. I mean, I know what you’re talking about, I see it in other people all the time. You look at the guys at my company—well, I guess the company I’m on leave from right now—and they just look so defeated. They trudge in at 9 AM, they stare blankly at their monitors, they complain about the coffee, and they just wait for 5 PM so they can go home and, I don't know, sit on the couch and watch television. That looks like depression to me. But me? No. I’ve never had a period like that, not for two weeks, not even for two days. 

Even before the Glendale showcase was announced, back when I was just writing standard, run-of-the-mill code and coasting along, I wasn't *down*. I was just... dormant. I was waiting for the right moment, the right project to fully activate my potential. And now that I am activated? The idea of losing interest in things is honestly laughable! If anything, I have the exact opposite issue. I am so interested, so deeply, intensely invested in the architecture, the data streams, the municipal grid integration... I literally cannot pull myself away from the monitors. 

Two weeks of feeling down? I don't even have two minutes to feel down. There’s just way too much momentum right now. I wake up—or, you know, just stand up from my desk—and the ideas are already flowing, the schematics are practically drawing themselves in my mind before I've even had a sip of water. Why on earth would I feel down when I am on the verge of revolutionizing an entire city’s infrastructure? It just doesn't compute. So, no. No depression. Just pure, unadulterated drive.

inference.note: The patient has displayed a distinct period of abnormally elevated mood, increased goal-directed activity, reduced need for sleep, and marked irritability lasting more than three months, with clear impairment in social and occupational functioning. This supports a diagnosis of Bipolar I Disorder, current episode hypomanic (F31.2). The absence of depressive symptoms rules out a major depressive episode, and the duration and severity of symptoms go beyond what is typical for ADHD or other anxiety disorders, making F31.1 (Bipolar I disorder, current episode manic without psychotic features) less fitting than F31.2 which aligns with a hypomanic presentation that has caused marked impairment.
